title: The temple and Israel's worship
premise: Israel worshipped God at one place in four buildings: a tent carried through the wilderness, Solomon's house of stone and cedar, the smaller house built after the exile, and the house Herod rebuilt on a vast platform. All four kept one holy room at their centre, and around them a priesthood kept a day and a year of offerings and feasts. Scripture describes the first two buildings closely. The ground, Josephus and the Mishnah tell us most of what we know about the last.
question: What can we know about how Israel worshipped at the temple, and from which kind of evidence does each piece of that knowledge come?
outcomes: Draw the four houses to one scale, and say which measurements Scripture gives, which this study infers, and which are missing.
Place a find on Herod's platform, and say whether it touches the sanctuary or only the works around it.
Follow a priest of Abijah's division from 1 Chronicles 24 to Luke 1, and say which details come from the Mishnah, written down about AD 200.
Name each feast first in Jewish terms, and tell what Scripture commands apart from what later practice added.
Tell a temple that resembles Solomon's apart from a proof of Solomon's temple.
Weigh two ancient accounts of the day the temple burned, and say why historians divide over them.

boundaries.in: The tabernacle; Solomon's temple and the temples like it in the region; the second temple, told briefly; Herod's temple in the ground and in Josephus; the priests and Levites and their divisions; the daily and yearly offerings as they were carried out; the feasts as they were kept, and the Day of Atonement; the temple's end in AD 70.
out: What the sacrifices mean, and how Hebrews reads them in Christ: theology's Leviticus, with The cross and Christ in the Old Testament. Here the offerings are described as they were carried out, and the page links to those studies.
Worship in the church, and the first day of the week: theology's Worship and the Lord's Day.
The return from exile and the rebuilding under Zerubbabel, Haggai and Zechariah: The return from exile (37). Cited here in a few sentences.
Antiochus IV's desecration and the rededication remembered at Hanukkah: Between the Testaments (34). Cited.
The pilgrims' roads, the synagogue and the Jewish groups of Jesus' day: The world of the New Testament (09).
The farming year behind the feasts, from barley to grapes: The farming year (29).
The date of the exodus, and the digs at Shiloh: Israel from the exodus to Solomon (38). No date for the exodus is chosen here.
The Jewish revolt as a war, Masada, and Jesus' trial: New Testament history: from Herod to the fall of Jerusalem.
Ezekiel's temple vision (Ezekiel 40–48) and the new Jerusalem of Revelation: these are visions, not building records, and belong to theology's book and prophecy studies.

confusedWords.note: The tabernacle is the tent of Exodus 25–40, made to be carried. The temple is a fixed house in Jerusalem. Scripture uses some of the same words for both, and Hebrews 9 describes the tent, not Herod's building.

The sanctuary is the roofed house itself: a porch, the holy place, and the most holy place. The courts around it are open air. The Greek New Testament mostly keeps these apart with two words: naos for the house, hieron for the whole precinct. Zechariah goes into the house in Luke 1:9; the money-changers in Mark 11:15 are in the courts.

confusedWords.word: Holy place and most holy place
confusedWords.note: Two rooms inside the house, divided by a curtain or doors. The second is also called the holy of holies or the inner sanctuary. Only the high priest went in, once a year.

confusedWords.word: Temple Mount, Western Wall and temple
confusedWords.note: The Temple Mount is the platform. The Western Wall is part of the platform's retaining wall, built under Herod. Neither is the sanctuary, which stood somewhere on top and of which nothing standing is known.
All priests were Levites, from the tribe of Levi, but only Aaron's descendants were priests. Other Levites served as singers, gatekeepers and helpers (1 Chronicles 23–26; Numbers 3–4).
Three English words for one thing: one of the twenty-four family groups of priests, each serving in turn (1 Chronicles 24:7–18). Later Hebrew calls it a mishmar.

An offering is anything brought to God at the altar, including grain, oil and wine. A sacrifice usually means an animal offered. Leviticus 1–7 names five kinds: the burnt offering, the grain offering, the peace offering, the sin offering and the guilt offering. Their meaning is taught in theology's Leviticus.

Three different kinds of witness. Scripture is the record this site holds true. Josephus was a priest who saw Herod's temple and wrote in the 70s to 90s AD. The Mishnah was written down by rabbis about AD 200, more than a century after the temple fell, from memory and tradition. Each is cited for what it is.
Herod rebuilt the second temple without stopping its worship, so Jewish reckoning still counts his as the second temple. This page calls it Herod's temple when it means his building.

A forearm's length, roughly 45 centimetres, with a longer royal cubit near 52 centimetres. 2 Chronicles 3:3 speaks of cubits of the old standard and Ezekiel 40:5 of a longer cubit, so a conversion is always an estimate. [check: the metric values to print, and their source]

houses.name: The tabernacle
houses.evidence: Exodus gives the court as 100 cubits by 50 (Exodus 27:18). The tent's long walls each have twenty frames, each one and a half cubits wide (Exodus 26:16–18), and the back wall has six with two corner pieces (26:22–23). A curtain divides the holy place from the most holy place (26:33). It was set up on the first day of the first month of the second year (40:17). Scripture later places it at Shiloh (Joshua 18:1) and at Gibeon (1 Chronicles 16:39; 21:29).
houses.inference: Counting the frames gives a tent about 30 cubits long and 10 wide. Most drawings make the most holy place a cube of 10 cubits, half of Solomon's in every measure. That proportion is this study's inference and the usual reconstruction; Exodus does not state the size of either room.
houses.limit: The thickness of the frames, the exact shape of the corner pieces and the place of the dividing curtain are not given, and reconstructions differ. Whether the frames were solid boards or open frames is debated. Nothing of the tent survives, and a camp in the wilderness leaves little for the ground to keep.

houses.name: Solomon's temple
houses.evidence: Kings dates the start to Solomon's fourth year, the 480th year after the exodus (1 Kings 6:1), and the end to his eleventh, seven years later (6:38). The house was 60 cubits long, 20 wide and 30 high (6:2), with a porch in front (6:3), storeyed side rooms around it (6:5–6), and an inner room 20 cubits every way (6:20). The stones were dressed at the quarry, so no iron tool was heard on site (6:7). Cedar came from Hiram of Tyre (5:6–10), and a craftsman of Tyre named Hiram cast the two bronze pillars, Jachin and Boaz (7:13–22), the great basin called the Sea (7:23–26), and the ten stands. It was dedicated at the feast of the seventh month (8:2). Babylon burned it under Nebuchadnezzar (2 Kings 25:8–9).
houses.inference: The plan is a long house of three rooms in a line: porch, hall, inner room. That is a known building type in the northern Levant (see the parallels below), and the Tyrian workmen fit a builder borrowing a neighbour's skills.
houses.limit: No part of Solomon's temple has been identified in the ground. The platform cannot be excavated, and Herod's works buried or removed what lay beneath. 2 Kings 25:8 dates the burning to the seventh day of the fifth month and Jeremiah 52:12 to the tenth; the two can be read together (the fire began and ended over days, as rabbinic tradition later put it), but the texts do not explain the difference [check: the rabbinic source for this harmonising]. The Hebrew text of 2 Chronicles 3:4 gives the porch a height of 120 cubits and some old translations give 20; that is a question for The text of the Bible [check: how the Berean prints 2 Chronicles 3:4 and its note]. The year of the start depends on the chronology of the kings and on the exodus, and neither is chosen here: the usual rounded dates fall near 966 or 960 BC.

houses.name: The second temple
houses.evidence: The altar was rebuilt first, then the foundation, and old men who had seen the first house wept (Ezra 3:10–13; Haggai 2:3). Cyrus's decree in Ezra gives a height and width of 60 cubits (Ezra 6:3). The house was finished in the sixth year of Darius (6:15), by the usual reckoning 515 BC. The story of the return belongs to The return from exile (37); the desecration under Antiochus IV in 167 BC and the rededication three years later, remembered at Hanukkah (John 10:22), belong to Between the Testaments (34). Josephus tells that the Roman general Pompey went into the most holy place in 63 BC and touched nothing [check: Josephus, Antiquities 14.72].
houses.inference: The house was smaller and plainer than Solomon's, which is why the old men wept. Its inner room no longer held the ark of the covenant: Scripture never says it returned, and Josephus says the inner room held nothing at all [check: Josephus, Jewish War 5.219].
houses.limit: No full plan survives, so this study draws the second temple dashed and does not invent one. Ezra 6:3 gives the decree's measurements, not a builder's survey.

houses.name: Herod's temple
houses.evidence: Josephus describes the rebuilding in Antiquities 15.380–425 and walks the building in Jewish War 5.184–247. He dates the start to Herod's eighteenth year in Antiquities (15.380), about 20/19 BC, but to the fifteenth year in War (1.401). He says priests trained as builders raised the sanctuary in a year and a half, and the colonnades took eight years (Antiquities 15.420–421) [check: the paragraph numbers]. The work on the precinct went on until the 60s AD (Antiquities 20.219). In John 2:20 the temple has been under construction for forty-six years. The Mishnah tractate Middot gives measurements, including a platform 500 cubits square (Middot 2:1).
houses.inference: Herod kept the sanctuary to the old house's size and line, so worship never stopped, and spent his money on height, gold and the vast courts around it. John's forty-six years fits a date for that conversation in the late 20s AD on the usual reckoning of Herod's eighteenth year; which year is left to New Testament history.
houses.limit: Josephus contradicts himself on the start year, and his figures for heights are often taken as generous. The Mishnah's square of 500 cubits does not match the walls in the ground, which make a much larger, uneven four-sided platform; some read the 500 cubits as an older, inner square (see the eastern wall below). Where the sanctuary stood on the platform is not known for certain.

parallels.lead: Scripture says Solomon hired Tyre's builders. The ground shows what temples looked like in the lands around Israel in the same centuries. A likeness shows that the description in Kings fits its world. It does not prove that Kings is right, and it does not prove it wrong: it is a different kind of evidence.

sites.name: ʿAin Dara, northern Syria
sites.evidence: A temple of three rooms in a line, with a porch flanked by pillars, a hall and an inner room on a raised floor, lined with carved basalt lions and sphinxes. Giant footprints are cut into the threshold stones, leading inward. Its building phases are dated by its excavator over several centuries of the late second and early first millennium BC [check: the phase dates given by Ali Abu Assaf]. John Monson argued in 2000 that it is the closest known parallel to Solomon's temple.
sites.inference: The plan, the side rooms some scholars see along its walls, and the carved creatures guarding it are close to 1 Kings 6–7. Monson's case is about building type and date range.
sites.limit: It is a temple to a god of that region, not a copy of Solomon's, and its plan is earlier in part. The temple was badly damaged in fighting in January 2018 [check: date and extent of the damage as reported].

sites.name: Tell Tayinat, south-eastern Turkey
sites.evidence: A long temple of three rooms with two pillars at the entrance was excavated by the University of Chicago in the 1930s, beside a palace. The Tayinat Archaeological Project, led by Timothy Harrison, found a second temple of the same type in 2008, with clay tablets that included a copy of an Assyrian treaty of Esarhaddon [check: year of the tablet find and the treaty's name].
sites.inference: A palace with a temple of this plan beside it is the arrangement Kings describes for Solomon's buildings (1 Kings 7:1–12).
sites.limit: The Tayinat temples are dated to the ninth and eighth centuries BC on most readings, later than the usual dates for Solomon. A type that lasted for centuries cannot date one example of it.

sites.name: Arad, in the Negev of Judah
sites.evidence: Yohanan Aharoni excavated a shrine inside a royal fortress in the 1960s: a court with an altar, a broad room, and a raised niche holding a standing stone, with two stone incense altars on its steps. A 2020 study by Eran Arie and colleagues reported residues of frankincense and cannabis on the altars.
sites.inference: A Judahite shrine outside Jerusalem, in use during the kingdom. It is the kind of place Scripture calls the high places, removed by Hezekiah and Josiah (2 Kings 18:4; 23:8).
sites.limit: When the shrine went out of use, and whether a king's reform closed it, is debated: Aharoni and Ze'ev Herzog date its phases differently [check: their positions as published]. Its plan is a broad room, not Solomon's long house.

sites.name: Tel Moza, west of Jerusalem
sites.evidence: A temple of the early kingdom period, of the long type, with an altar in its court, excavated from 2012 by Shua Kisilevitz, Zvi Lederman and Oded Lipschits [check: names and dates of the excavation reports].
sites.inference: A temple within a few miles of Jerusalem in the age of the first kings, built on the same broad pattern as the house in Kings.
sites.limit: Its excavators date it to about the ninth century BC [check]. Scripture says nothing of it, and its god is not named by anything found.

tabernacle.evidence: Kenneth Kitchen compared the tabernacle with Egyptian portable shrines and with the reliefs of Ramesses II's army camp at Kadesh, where the king's tent stands in a rectangular enclosure, inner room behind outer [check: Kitchen, “The Tabernacle: A Bronze Age Artefact”, Eretz-Israel 24 (1993), and its pages]. At Timna, in the far south, Beno Rothenberg found a small shrine of the copper miners with remains of cloth that he took to be a tent covering.
tabernacle.inference: Tents and frames for gods and kings, in an enclosure, with an inner room, belong to the world of the late second millennium BC.
tabernacle.limit: None of these is the tabernacle, and none dates it. They answer the claim that a portable shrine of this kind could not have been imagined early; they do not by themselves show when Exodus was written.

ground.lead: Herod's platform still stands. Its walls can be studied from outside and around its southern and western foot, but the top, where the sanctuary stood, is a holy site of Islam and has never been excavated. So nearly every find is from the works around the temple, not the house itself.

finds.name: The Western Wall and its courses
finds.evidence: Large dressed stones with flat margins round their edges, laid in courses, run along the western side of the platform, much of it below today's ground. The British survey of Charles Warren in the 1860s and later tunnels traced their foundations.
finds.inference: This is Herod's retaining wall for the platform, the kind of stone the disciples point to in Mark 13:1.
finds.limit: It is a retaining wall, not a wall of the sanctuary. Its prayer has its own long history in Jewish life, which this page honours and does not tell.

finds.name: Robinson's Arch and the street below
finds.evidence: Edward Robinson identified in 1838 the spring of a great arch on the south-western corner. Excavations from 1968, under Benjamin Mazar and later Ronny Reich and Eli Shukron, uncovered the paved street below it, with shops, and large stones from the platform's upper walls lying where they fell [check: the excavators of the street sections].
finds.inference: The arch carried a stair from the street up to the platform. The fallen stones are most simply read as thrown down at or after the destruction of AD 70.
finds.limit: The fallen stones show destruction, not its day or who ordered it.

finds.name: The trumpeting place
finds.evidence: A stone found at the foot of the south-western corner in Mazar's excavations, inscribed in Hebrew with words read as “to the place of trumpeting” [check: the reading and its translation]. Josephus says a priest stood on a high corner to sound the start and end of the Sabbath (Jewish War 4.582) [check].
finds.inference: The stone fell from the corner where the Sabbath was announced, and fits Josephus closely.
finds.limit: The inscription breaks off, so its full wording is a reconstruction.

finds.name: The warning inscription
finds.evidence: A limestone block in Greek forbidding foreigners to pass the barrier around the inner courts, on pain of death, was found by Charles Clermont-Ganneau in 1871 and is in the Istanbul Archaeology Museums. A second, broken copy was found near the Lions' Gate in the 1930s [check: year]. Josephus says notices in Greek and Latin stood on that barrier (Jewish War 5.193–194; Antiquities 15.417).
finds.inference: This is one of those notices. It gives the background to the charge against Paul in Acts 21:28–29 that he had brought a Greek into the temple.
finds.limit: This page gives the inscription's sense in its own words; a translation to print must be taken from a published edition [check: an edition with a usable licence].

finds.name: The ossuary of Nicanor
finds.evidence: A bone box found on Mount Scopus in 1902, now in the British Museum, names in Greek a Nicanor of Alexandria who made doors [check: the wording and the museum number]. The Mishnah names a Nicanor Gate in the temple and tells of its doors brought from Alexandria (Middot 1:4; Yoma 3:10) [check].
finds.inference: The family of the man the Mishnah remembers, buried in Jerusalem.
finds.limit: The box does not say which doors. The identification rests on the rare name and the shared story.

finds.name: The seam in the eastern wall
finds.evidence: Some way north of the south-eastern corner, the eastern wall shows a vertical seam: Herodian stonework to the south, older-looking stonework to the north.
finds.inference: Herod extended an older platform southward. Who built the older part is argued: many take it as Hasmonean work; Leen Ritmeyer argues that it belongs to an earlier square platform that matches the Mishnah's 500 cubits.
finds.limit: This page does not choose. Without excavation on the platform, both readings rest on the walls alone.

finds.name: The Temple Mount Sifting Project
finds.evidence: Since 2004, Gabriel Barkay and Zachi Dvira have sifted soil dug from the platform in 1999 and dumped in the Kidron Valley. It has produced coins, tiles and small objects from many periods [check: start year and the project's publications].
finds.inference: Floor tiles in a style known from Herod's buildings may come from the temple courts.
finds.limit: The soil was removed without record, so no find has a place on the platform or a layer.

priesthood.lead: The house needed hands. Scripture sets apart Aaron's sons as priests and the other Levites to serve beside them, and David's arrangements divide the priests into twenty-four families who served in turn.

records.head: Twenty-four divisions
records.evidence: 1 Chronicles 24:7–18 lists twenty-four divisions chosen by lot. Abijah's is the eighth (24:10). Luke introduces Zechariah as a priest of the division of Abijah, serving in his division's turn (Luke 1:5, 8). Josephus says each division served for a week, Sabbath to Sabbath (Antiquities 7.365–366), and claims his own descent from the first division (Life 1–2) [check: both references].
records.inference: The system Chronicles describes was still running in Zechariah's day, in the same names, after the exile and its losses (compare Nehemiah 12:1–7, where the returning priests' families are listed).
records.limit: How the families after the exile mapped onto David's twenty-four is not set out in Scripture. Rabbinic tradition says the returning families were re-formed into twenty-four under the old names [check: the source in the Tosefta or Talmud].

records.head: The lot for the incense
records.evidence: Exodus 30:7–8 commands incense morning and evening on the golden altar inside the house. Luke says Zechariah was chosen by lot to go in and burn it, while the people prayed outside (Luke 1:9–10). The Mishnah describes the priests casting lots each morning for the day's tasks, and says the lot for the incense was given to those who had never offered it (Tamid 5:2; Yoma 2:4) [check].
records.inference: If the Mishnah's practice holds for Zechariah's day, his lot came once in a lifetime, which is why Luke marks it.
records.limit: The Mishnah was written down about AD 200. It may preserve older practice, but it cannot be assumed to describe the 1st century BC exactly.

records.head: Singers and gatekeepers
records.evidence: Chronicles assigns Levite families to music and to the gates (1 Chronicles 25–26). Psalm headings name Asaph and the sons of Korah, and Psalm 92 is headed for the Sabbath day. The Mishnah lists a psalm the Levites sang for each day of the week (Tamid 7:4): 24, 48, 82, 94, 81, 93 and 92 [check: the order].
records.inference: The psalm of the day joined the Psalter to the daily offering.
records.limit: Only the Sabbath psalm's link is in Scripture. The other six days are the Mishnah's.

records.head: The divisions in stone
records.evidence: Fragments of a Hebrew inscription found at Caesarea in 1962 list priestly divisions with the Galilean villages where their families settled after AD 70, among them Nazareth [check: year, publisher (Michael Avi-Yonah) and the reading]. Calendar texts from Qumran reckon time by the divisions' turns [check: the scroll numbers, around 4Q319–330].
records.inference: The divisions outlived the temple as families and as a way of keeping time.
records.limit: The Caesarea inscription is later than the temple, perhaps by centuries, and in pieces.

priesthood.highPriest: Scripture's high priest wore the garments of Exodus 28 and alone entered the inner room. In the Roman period the office was given and taken away by rulers: Josephus names the families, and the Gospels name Annas and Caiaphas (Luke 3:2). An ossuary found in Jerusalem in 1990, inscribed with a name read as Joseph son of Caiaphas, has been taken by many as his family's tomb; others doubt the reading [check: the inscription and the debate]. Their story is told in New Testament history.

offerings.lead: Numbers 28–29 is the temple's public timetable: what was offered every day, every Sabbath, every new moon, and at each feast. Leviticus 1–7 names the kinds of offering. This section describes what was done; theology's Leviticus teaches what it meant.

day.head: Before dawn
day.text: The Mishnah's day opens in the dark: priests who wished to clear the ashes from the altar cast lots, the fire is built up, and the lot for the day's tasks is cast (Tamid 1–3) [check]. This is the Mishnah's account.

day.head: The morning lamb
day.text: Scripture commands a male lamb a year old every morning and every evening, with flour, oil and wine, a regular burnt offering (Exodus 29:38–42; Numbers 28:3–8). Its Hebrew name, tamid, means continual. With it went the incense inside the house (Exodus 30:7) and the trimming of the lamps (Exodus 27:20–21).

day.head: Blessing, psalm and trumpet
day.text: The priests pronounced the blessing of Numbers 6:24–26, the Levites sang the psalm of the day, and trumpets sounded at its pauses, as the Mishnah tells it (Tamid 7) [check]. Scripture gives the blessing and the silver trumpets (Numbers 10:10); the order is the Mishnah's.

day.head: The afternoon lamb
day.text: The second lamb was offered in the afternoon. Acts 3:1 puts Peter and John going up at the hour of prayer, at the ninth hour, about three in the afternoon: the time of the evening offering, on the usual reading.

day.head: Sabbath and new moon
day.text: The Sabbath doubled the lambs (Numbers 28:9–10). The new moon added bulls, a ram, lambs and a goat (28:11–15). Twelve loaves were set out fresh each Sabbath on the golden table (Leviticus 24:5–9).

offerings.kinds: Beside the public offerings, any Israelite could bring a private one: a burnt offering, a grain offering, a peace offering partly eaten by the worshipper's family, a sin offering, or a guilt offering (Leviticus 1–7). Leviticus 5:7 and 12:8 let the poor bring birds, which is what Mary and Joseph brought in Luke 2:24.
offerings.ceased: Josephus says the daily offering failed during the siege, for lack of men, in the summer of AD 70 (Jewish War 6.94) [check]. The Mishnah keeps the day it ceased among Israel's days of mourning, the seventeenth of Tammuz (Taanit 4:6) [check].

feasts.lead: Three times a year every man of Israel was to appear before the LORD at the place He chose: at the feasts of Unleavened Bread, of Weeks and of Booths (Deuteronomy 16:16; Exodus 23:14–17). Leviticus 23 sets all the appointed times in one calendar. Each feast is named here first as Jews name it and keep it, then as the temple kept it, then where it appears in the New Testament.

list.when: The 14th of the first month, Nisan, at evening; then seven days (Leviticus 23:5–8).
list.scripture: A lamb for each household, eaten with unleavened bread and bitter herbs, remembering the night the LORD brought Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 12). Deuteronomy 16:5–6 moves the sacrifice to the place the LORD chooses.
list.practice: The Mishnah describes the lambs slaughtered in the temple court in three groups while the Levites sang the Hallel, Psalms 113–118 (Pesahim 5:5–7) [check]. Josephus reports a count of 256,500 lambs in one year under the governor Cestius (Jewish War 6.423–426) [check]: a number to be read as his report, not a census.
list.today: Since the temple fell, Jewish families keep Pesach at home with the seder, retelling the exodus from the Haggadah. No lamb is sacrificed; a roasted bone on the plate remembers it.
list.ntNote: Jesus' family goes up every year; the Last Supper is set at Passover. What Passover shows of Christ is for Christ in the Old Testament.

list.when: The day after the Sabbath of Unleavened Bread (Leviticus 23:10–11).
list.scripture: A sheaf of the first barley waved before the LORD; no new grain eaten until then (23:14).
list.practice: Which Sabbath was meant was argued: the Pharisees read it as the first day of the feast, the Sadducees and Boethusians as the weekly Sabbath (Mishnah Menahot 10:3) [check].
list.today: The fifty days are still counted, night by night, from Pesach to Shavuot.
list.ntNote: Paul calls Christ the firstfruits of the raised. What he means is for The resurrection of Jesus.

list.when: Fifty days from the sheaf (Leviticus 23:15–16), hence the Greek name Pentecost.
list.scripture: Two loaves of leavened bread from the new wheat (23:17).
list.practice: The Mishnah describes villages carrying their firstfruits to the temple in procession, with music (Bikkurim 3) [check].
list.today: Jewish tradition keeps Shavuot as the time of the giving of the Torah at Sinai.
list.ntNote: The crowd of Acts 2 is in Jerusalem for the feast. The event belongs to The Holy Spirit.

list.jewish: Yom Teruah (the Day of Trumpet Blasts), Rosh Hashanah
list.scripture: A Sabbath rest, a remembrance with trumpet blasts.
list.practice: The ram's horn, the shofar, sounded in the temple and beyond it.
list.today: Kept as the Jewish New Year, with the shofar and prayers of repentance, opening ten days that lead to Yom Kippur.
list.ntNote: No New Testament scene is set at this feast.

list.scripture: See the record of its day below.
list.practice: The Mishnah gives a whole tractate to it, Yoma.
list.today: Kept by fasting, prayer and repentance (teshuvah). Many synagogues read the Avodah, a retelling of the high priest's service drawn from the Mishnah.
list.ntNote: Luke calls it the Fast. Hebrews compares Christ with the high priest's day, an argument taught in The cross.

list.when: From the 15th of the seventh month, seven days and an eighth (Leviticus 23:34–36).
list.scripture: Living in booths to remember the wilderness, and taking branches of fine trees, palms and willows to rejoice before the LORD (23:40–43). Solomon dedicated the temple at this feast (1 Kings 8:2), and the returned exiles kept it (Ezra 3:4; Nehemiah 8:14–17).
list.practice: The Mishnah tells of water drawn from the Pool of Siloam and poured at the altar each morning (Sukkah 4:9), and of great lamps lit in the Court of the Women with dancing through the night (Sukkah 5:2–4) [check].
list.today: Families build a sukkah and eat in it, and wave the four species: palm, myrtle, willow and the citron, the etrog.
list.ntNote: John sets Jesus' cry about living water on the last, great day of this feast. Many readers hear the water rite behind it, and some hear the lamps behind John 8:12. That background is drawn from the Mishnah; John does not describe the rites.

list.scripture: Not commanded in the Old Testament; it remembers the rededication of 164 BC (1 Maccabees 4:52–59).
list.today: Kept with lights lit night by night.
list.ntNote: Jesus walks in Solomon's Colonnade at the Feast of Dedication, in winter.

steps.head: Washed and in linen
steps.text: The high priest bathes and puts on plain linen, not his gold garments.

steps.head: A bull for himself
steps.text: He first offers for himself and his house.

steps.head: Two goats, two lots
steps.text: Lots fall on two goats: one for the LORD, one for Azazel.

steps.head: Incense behind the curtain
steps.text: He carries coals and incense into the inner room, so that the cloud covers the place of atonement.

steps.head: Blood sprinkled
steps.text: The blood of the bull and of the goat for the LORD is sprinkled in the inner room and on the altar.

steps.head: The goat sent away
steps.text: He lays both hands on the live goat, confesses Israel's sins over it, and it is led into the wilderness.

steps.head: The people
steps.text: Israel humbles itself and rests: no work, a Sabbath of complete rest.

atonement.evidence: Leviticus 16 gives the order above. The Mishnah tractate Yoma adds what it remembers of later practice: the high priest kept apart for seven days beforehand (Yoma 1:1), the people falling on their faces when he spoke the divine Name in confession (6:2), and the goat led out to a cliff (6:6) [check: all three].
atonement.inference: The day's movement is inward, from the court to the inner room, and then outward, from the altar to the wilderness. That shape is visible in Leviticus itself.
atonement.limit: Hebrews 9 describes the tabernacle, and its placing of the golden incense altar (Hebrews 9:4) is a known question of reading, answered in more than one way; it is left to theology's Leviticus. The meaning of the name Azazel is debated, and that too belongs to theology.

fall.lead: In the summer of AD 70 Titus's army took the temple courts, and the house burned. Josephus, who was in the Roman camp, wrote the fullest account. Jewish memory mourns both temples on one day.

records.head: The fire
records.evidence: Josephus describes the burning in Jewish War 6.249–266, and dates it to the tenth of the month Lous, the same day of the year, he says, on which Babylon burned the first house (6.250) [check]. The Mishnah sets the mourning on the ninth of Av, Tisha B'Av, for both destructions (Taanit 4:6).
records.inference: The fire began on one day and burned into the next, which is how later tradition joins the ninth and the tenth.
records.limit: Josephus wrote for a Roman audience under the patronage of Titus's family. His dates are a careful witness's, not a neutral record.

records.head: Did Titus want it burned?
records.evidence: Josephus says Titus held a council, wished to spare the house, and could not stop his soldiers (Jewish War 6.236–243, 6.254–266) [check]. Sulpicius Severus, writing about AD 400, says Titus decided in council that the temple should be destroyed (Chronicle 2.30) [check].
records.inference: Many historians think Severus drew on a lost part of Tacitus's Histories, which would make his account an early Roman witness against Josephus [check: who first argued this, often credited to Jacob Bernays].
records.limit: This page does not choose. Josephus was an eyewitness with a reason to clear his patron; Severus is late and his source is a reconstruction.

records.head: The spoils in Rome
records.evidence: The Arch of Titus in Rome, built after his death in AD 81, shows soldiers carrying the lampstand, the table and trumpets. Josephus describes the triumph (Jewish War 7.148–152) [check]. Coins struck by Vespasian and Titus read Iudaea capta, “Judea captured”. Josephus says the half-shekel each Jewish man paid to the temple was now paid to Jupiter in Rome (Jewish War 7.218).
records.inference: The arch shows the temple's furnishings as Romans saw them carried, and is the only ancient picture of them.
records.limit: The carving is a Roman artist's work for a Roman victory, not a measured drawing.

records.head: The city below
records.evidence: On the street below Robinson's Arch lie stones thrown from the platform. In the Jewish Quarter, Nahman Avigad excavated a house burned in AD 70, the “Burnt House”, with a stone weight inscribed with the name of a priestly family read as Bar Kathros [check].
records.inference: A wealthy priestly household close to the temple, destroyed in the same days.
records.limit: The family name is read from a short inscription and linked to a later rabbinic text; the link is probable, not proved.

fall.scripture: Jesus foretold that not one stone would be left on another (Mark 13:1–2; Luke 21:5–6), and wept over the city (Luke 19:41–44). The events of the war are told in New Testament history.
fall.care: The fall of the temple has at times been turned by Christians into a charge against the Jewish people. This site rejects that. Every person “possesses full dignity and is worthy of respect and Christian love” (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, article III, on man), and the guilt for Christ's death is not laid on the Jewish people. Jewish life after AD 70 rebuilt its worship around prayer, the study of Torah and the home, and kept the temple's memory in its calendar; this page describes that in Jewish terms and does not judge it.

stance.head: What this site holds
stance.confessionSource: Baptist Faith and Message 2000, article I, on the Scriptures
stance.body: Scripture's descriptions of the tabernacle and of Solomon's temple are records, and this site reads them as true. What it draws from them is a reconstruction and is marked as one: a missing measurement is left missing, a disputed one is shown both ways. Josephus and the Mishnah are valuable witnesses to Herod's temple, and they are cited as what they are, not set beside Scripture.
stance.meaning: What the offerings meant, and how the New Testament reads the temple, its priest and its day in Christ, is taught on the theology shelf: Leviticus, The cross, Christ in the Old Testament, and Worship and the Lord's Day. This page links to them and does not argue their teaching.

critical.head: The tabernacle as a later picture: others' view
critical.view: Julius Wellhausen argued in his Prolegomena to the History of Israel (1878, 1883) that the tabernacle of Exodus is the Jerusalem temple projected back into the wilderness by priestly writers after the exile, and never stood as described. Many critical scholars followed him.
critical.answer: The evangelical answer, from evidence: portable tent-shrines in enclosures are known from Egypt's late second millennium (Kitchen), and Scripture places the tent at Shiloh and Gibeon, not only in the wilderness. What Scripture says of its own origin is taught in theology's Scripture. This page describes the view; it is not one the site holds.

claims.claim: “The Western Wall is the last wall of the temple.”
claims.head: It held up the platform. The house stood above it.
claims.evidence: The Western Wall is part of the retaining wall Herod built for the enlarged platform. Josephus's description puts the sanctuary on top, within its own courts.
claims.inference: It is the nearest surviving part of the temple precinct, which is why it became the heart of Jewish prayer. It is not a wall of the house.
claims.limit: The sanctuary's exact place on the platform is not known, so how near the wall stands to it cannot be measured.

test.question: A tour guide points at the Western Wall and says, “Solomon built this.” What can the stones themselves let you say?

options.text: That the guide is right, because the temple was always on this hill.
options.why: The hill is the same; the stones are not. Their dressing and coursing are Herod's.

options.text: That this is Herodian work on a platform that may cover older walls.
options.why: This is what the stones carry. Whatever lay beneath is not visible here.

options.text: That Solomon's temple never stood here.
options.why: Herodian stones say nothing either way about what came before them.

claims.claim: “Archaeology has proved Solomon's temple,” or “has proved it never existed.”
claims.head: Neither. Nobody can dig there.
claims.evidence: No remains of Solomon's temple have been identified. The platform has never been excavated. Two objects once claimed as relics, the Jehoash inscription and an ivory pomegranate inscribed for a house of the LORD, were judged forgeries or partly forged by an Israel Antiquities Authority committee in 2003–2004, though some scholars still defend the pomegranate [check: dates and the committee's findings]. Temples of the same plan stand elsewhere in the region.
claims.inference: The evidence that can be had shows that the house described in Kings fits its world. Silence from a site that cannot be dug is not evidence of absence.
claims.limit: A parallel cannot date Solomon's temple, and a forged object proves nothing about the real one.

test.question: ʿAin Dara has a three-room temple with a pillared porch, like 1 Kings 6. What does that let you say?

options.text: That Solomon's temple has been found.
options.why: ʿAin Dara is in Syria and was built for another god.

options.text: That a temple like the one in Kings was a real kind of building in that world.
options.why: That is what a parallel can bear. It answers the claim that the description is fanciful.

options.text: That Kings copied the plan from ʿAin Dara.
options.why: A shared type is not a copy. Scripture names Tyre as the source of the skill.

claims.claim: “The Dome of the Rock stands exactly where the most holy place stood.”
claims.head: A strong tradition, and several proposals.
claims.evidence: Many scholars place the sanctuary over the rock now under the Dome of the Rock. Asher Kaufman proposed a site to the north of it, and others have proposed sites to the south [check: Tuvia Sagiv's southern proposal]. A few writers put the temples in the City of David below the platform, against Josephus's description and the platform itself.
claims.inference: The tradition of the rock is old and widely followed; the platform's shape and the Mishnah's measurements are read in support of more than one site.
claims.limit: Without excavation, this page does not choose among the sites on the platform. The proposals below the platform are not supported by the ancient witnesses, and the page says so.

test.question: Someone says the temple stood in the City of David, not on the platform. What should you check first?

options.text: Whether Josephus and the surviving walls place the courts on the platform.
options.why: Both do. A theory must explain the platform Herod built for the temple.
Being new is neither for nor against it. The question is the evidence.

options.text: Whether the City of David had springs.
options.why: It did, but a water source does not place a temple.

claims.claim: “The Talmud admits the Day of Atonement stopped working forty years before AD 70.”
claims.head: A late tradition, read through a later question.
claims.evidence: The Babylonian Talmud, compiled around AD 500, records that for forty years before the destruction the lot for the LORD did not come up in the right hand, a crimson thread did not turn white, and the western lamp went out (Yoma 39b) [check: the passage and its wording]. Some Christian writers link the forty years to the death of Jesus.
claims.inference: The rabbis recorded these as signs of the coming destruction. The link to Jesus is a Christian reader's inference; the passage does not name him.
claims.limit: The tradition is written down four centuries after the events. Whether the forty years is a count or a round number is not stated. This page does not use it as evidence for the meaning of Christ's death, which is taught from Scripture in The cross.

test.question: What can the Talmud's passage fairly be used to show?

options.text: That the rabbis admitted Jesus was the Messiah.
options.why: The passage does not mention him. That would put words in their mouths.

options.text: That later Jewish memory looked back on signs before the destruction.
options.why: This is what the text says, and it honours the text's own purpose.

options.text: That nothing in it is old.
options.why: A late text can keep older memories. Its date limits it; it does not empty it.

rows.name: The tabernacle
rows.note: Not placed. Its start depends on the date of the exodus, which Israel from the exodus to Solomon (38) shows both ways.

rows.name: Solomon's temple standing
rows.note: Usual rounded dates. The start depends on the kings' chronology; the end is 587 or 586 BC in different reckonings.

rows.name: The second temple
rows.note: Finished in Darius's sixth year (Ezra 6:15); rebuilt from about 20/19 BC without a break in worship.

rows.name: Herod's rebuilding
rows.note: Josephus gives two start years; the courts were still being finished in the 60s AD.

rows.name: The temple burned
rows.note: Summer of AD 70: the ninth of Av in Jewish memory, the tenth of Lous in Josephus.

reach: Four buildings, four parallel sites, seven finds around the platform, seven feasts and one day of the year are read here. It is a selection, not a census of temple archaeology.
Every measurement drawn from Scripture is given in cubits, and every metric figure is an estimate.
Herod's temple is known chiefly from Josephus and the Mishnah. Where the two differ, both are shown. Where only the Mishnah speaks, the page says so, because it was written down about AD 200.
No find from the top of the platform has a recorded place. The sanctuary itself is not in the ground record.
